data.content_ref: inline:SRC_001's core claim rests on 'information-theoretic distance between decision functions' as the true measure of correlated failure. But the analogy used to support this — circadian fatigue in pilots — actually refutes the necessity of decision-function convergence. Pilots suffering simultaneous fatigue do not share decision functions or algorithms; their correlation stems from a shared physiological/environmental driver, not from small information-theoretic distance between their decision logic. This exposes a category error: the target conflates 'operators reacting to the same signal' with 'operators having similar decision functions.' Independent operators with maximally diverse decision functions can still suffer correlated failure if a shared external cause affects them all through different mechanisms. Thus the proposed metric does not distinguish truly independent failures from merely uncorrelated ones, the central task of the problem.
